title: Gurmukh and manmukh
hook: the one facing the Guru and the one facing only their own mind

segments.voice: Yesterday, maya, the passing pull; your line was pretty, and passing. Today, which way you're facing when it tugs.

Young sunflowers do something lovely. In the morning their heads turn east, toward the light, and by evening they've followed it west. Now suppose one sunflower decided to face a mirror instead. It would see a very handsome sunflower. It would also, slowly, stop growing. Where you face shapes what you become. The Guru Granth Sahib has two words for the two ways a person can face, and they appear on page after page. Today's word is the first of them: gurmukh.
screen: `A FIELD FACING EAST.` → `ONE FACING A MIRROR.` → `WHERE YOU FACE, YOU GROW.`

segments.voice: Gurmukh is two words joined: gur, the Guru, and mukh, the face, or the mouth. A gurmukh is someone whose face is turned toward the Guru. Its opposite is manmukh. Man is the mind, the restless self; a manmukh faces only their own mind, their own wants, their own reflection. Sikh teachers often read these less as two tribes of people, good ones and bad ones, than as two directions, and a person can turn either way in a single afternoon. The hymns paint them clearly. The manmukh is busy and anxious, driven by the five thieves we met a few days ago, always chasing the next thing, like someone wandering in the dark. The gurmukh has no special title. It's someone who listens to the Guru's word, remembers the Name, works honestly and serves, and so finds a kind of steadiness. Guru Nanak's great conversation with the yogis, the Sidh Gosht, keeps coming back to this word: it is through the Guru, facing the Guru, that one comes to understand. And for Sikhs, the Guru is now the Guru Granth Sahib, the Word itself. So facing the Guru can be as simple as opening the book, listening to a hymn, or letting a line of it question you before you act. The test is small. Before I do this, which way am I facing: toward what I'd do if I were listening to the Guru, or toward the mirror?
screen: `GUR + MUKH — FACING THE GURU.` · `MAN + MUKH — FACING YOUR OWN MIND.` · `TWO DIRECTIONS, NOT TWO TRIBES.` · `THE GURU IS NOW THE WORD.` · then, large: `FACE THE GURU.`

segments.voice: Think of one choice waiting for you, a message, a task, a conversation, and picture yourself turned toward the mirror, choosing only for your own comfort. Now turn, the way a sunflower turns, toward the best you know: truth, kindness, the Guru's word if that's your path. See how the choice looks from there, settle on one good turn, and rest with the breath.
Gurmukh. The one whose face is turned toward the Guru. Its opposite, manmukh, faces only its own mind. Anyone can turn either way.
Your line: face the guru. Where you face, you grow. Day two hundred forty-two, done.

howItsDone: Sikhs use gurmukh for a person oriented toward the Guru's teaching and manmukh for one led by their own mind; many turn to the Guru Granth Sahib, through daily reading or kirtan, as the way of facing the Guru.

original.note: Gurmukhi: gurmukh, the one facing the Guru; the script itself is called Gurmukhi, 'from the Guru's mouth'.

trapdoor: what you thought: a gurmukh is a very holy person with a title.
what it means: anyone whose face is turned toward the Guru's word, in that moment, rather than toward their own restless mind.
what a scholar hears: gur plus mukh (face, mouth); paired throughout the Granth with manmukh; the name of the Gurmukhi script is usually explained from the same word.
recall: recite and remember, again and again

'Two directions, not two tribes' is now given as how Sikh teachers read the pair, not as the Granth's own statement; cut 'here's the surprising part' (day 232 already taught the Granth as Guru).
